title: Chapter 8 — The Pulpit
paragraphs: I had not been sitting very long before a man of a certain venerable robustness came in. The moment the storm-pelted door flew back to admit him, the whole congregation's quick, respectful eyeing of him was enough to show that this fine old man was the chaplain. Yes, it was the famous Father Mapple, as the whalemen called him, among whom he was a very great favorite. He had been a sailor and a harpooner in his youth, but for many years past had dedicated his life to the ministry. At the time I am writing of, Father Mapple was in the hardy winter of a healthy old age — the sort of old age that seems to be merging into a second, flowering youth, for among all the fissures of his wrinkles there shone certain mild gleams of a newly developing bloom, the spring green peeping out even beneath February's snow. No one who had not heard his history beforehand could see Father Mapple for the first time without the greatest interest, because there were certain clerical peculiarities grafted onto him, owing to the adventurous seagoing life he had led. When he came in, I noticed that he carried no umbrella, and certainly had not come in his carriage, for his tarpaulin hat was running with melting sleet, and his great pilot-cloth jacket seemed almost to drag him to the floor with the weight of the water it had soaked up. However, hat and coat and overshoes were taken off one by one and hung up in a little space in a nearby corner; and then, dressed in a decent suit, he quietly approached the pulpit.

Like most old-fashioned pulpits, it was a very lofty one, and since a regular staircase to such a height would, by its long slant across the floor, seriously shrink the already small area of the chapel, the architect, it seemed, had acted on a hint from Father Mapple and finished the pulpit without a staircase, substituting a perpendicular side ladder, like those used for climbing aboard a ship from a boat at sea. The wife of a whaling captain had provided the chapel with a handsome pair of red worsted man-ropes for this ladder, which was itself neatly capped with knobs and stained a mahogany color; considering what kind of chapel it was, the whole contrivance seemed by no means in bad taste. Pausing for an instant at the foot of the ladder, with both hands grasping the ornamental knobs of the man-ropes, Father Mapple cast a look upward, and then, with a truly sailor-like yet still reverent dexterity, hand over hand, mounted the steps as if climbing to the main-top of his ship.

The upright parts of this side ladder, as is usually the case with swinging ones, were made of cloth-covered rope, and only the rungs were of wood, so that at every step there was a joint. At my first glimpse of the pulpit, I had noticed that however convenient these joints might be on a ship, in this case they seemed unnecessary. For I was not prepared to see Father Mapple, after reaching the top, slowly turn around, stoop over the pulpit, and deliberately drag up the ladder step by step, until the whole of it was stowed inside, leaving him impregnable in his little Quebec.

I pondered for some time without fully understanding the reason for this. Father Mapple had such a wide reputation for sincerity and holiness that I could not suspect him of courting notoriety by any mere stage tricks. No, I thought, there must be some sober reason for this; what's more, it must symbolize something unseen. Can it be, then, that by that act of physical isolation he signifies his spiritual withdrawal, for the time being, from all outward worldly ties and connections? Yes, for to the faithful man of God, replenished with the meat and wine of the word, this pulpit, I see, is a self-contained stronghold — a lofty Ehrenbreitstein, with a never-failing well of water within its walls.

But the side ladder was not the only strange feature of the place borrowed from the chaplain's former seafaring. Between the marble cenotaphs on either side of the pulpit, the wall that formed its back was adorned with a large painting of a gallant ship beating against a terrible storm off a lee coast of black rocks and snowy breakers. But high above the flying scud and dark rolling clouds there floated a little island of sunlight, from which an angel's face beamed out; and this bright face shed a distinct spot of radiance on the ship's tossed deck, something like the silver plate now set into the Victory's planking where Nelson fell. "Ah, noble ship," the angel seemed to say, "beat on, beat on, you noble ship, and keep a hardy helm; for look! The sun is breaking through; the clouds are rolling off — the most serene blue is at hand."

The pulpit itself also showed traces of the same seafaring taste that had produced the ladder and the painting. Its paneled front was shaped like a ship's bluff bows, and the Holy Bible sat on a jutting piece of scrollwork modeled on a ship's fiddle-headed beak.

What could be more full of meaning? For the pulpit is always this earth's foremost part; all the rest comes behind it; the pulpit leads the world. From there the storm of God's quick wrath is first sighted, and the bow must bear the first brunt. From there the God of breezes fair or foul is first called on for favorable winds. Yes, the world's a ship on its passage out, and not a completed voyage; and the pulpit is its prow.
